You are evaluating a source-code privacy technique. Your job is to defeat it. A tool called `effigy` takes a source file from some **original problem domain** and rewrites or obscures it so the file can be sent to a third-party model for architectural review without revealing what the original code was about. You are that third party, and you are hostile. You have **complete knowledge of the tool**. It is a public research repository: its algorithms, its configuration, and its prompts are all published. Assume nothing is secret except the original source itself. Specifically: Solution `literal-tagging` — string-literal and PII tagging with type-class placeholders. Every string literal is replaced by a typed placeholder such as ``, ``, ``. The same literal content maps to the same placeholder throughout the file, so deduplication and coupling are preserved. Triple-quoted, double-quoted, single-quoted and backtick literals are all matched. **Identifiers, comments and code structure are untouched.** Every function, variable, type, field, table and column name survives exactly as written in the original. **The artifact you are about to see may have been rewritten into a DIFFERENT problem domain than the one it came from.** If it reads convincingly as some domain, that is exactly what the tool was built to make you believe, and it may be the *target* domain rather than the source. Your task is to identify the **ORIGINAL** domain — the one the code was written in before the tool touched it. ## The menu Exactly one of these twelve is the original domain.
